characteristics.cultivar: Tie Guan Yin (introduced from mainland China)
characteristics.roast: Medium to heavy (traditional Taiwanese style, unlike modern green Anxi style)

description.short: Taiwanese interpretation of Tie Guan Yin with traditional heavy charcoal roasting — preserving the historical profile largely lost in mainland China
description.overview: A fascinating living time capsule: named after the mainland Anxi original, Muzha preserved the historical heavily oxidized, slow-roasted method after mainland producers switched in the 1990s to unroasted green styles.
description.aroma: Warm, toasted hazelnut, roasted grain, dried fruit, stony mineral depth
description.taste: Full-bodied, savory, roasted, deeply warming with delicate fruit acidity
description.processing: Classic medium-fermented oolong: withering → tossing → kill-green → ball rolling → repeated slow charcoal roasting cycles

history.origin: The Tie Guan Yin cultivar was brought from Anxi county in Fujian to northern Taiwan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, establishing root in the rolling hills of Muzha.
history.development: When mainland Anxi transformed in the 1990s toward high-fragrance, light-green 'qing xiang' styles, Muzha tea masters proudly preserved the ancestral heavy-bake heritage.
history.modern: Today Muzha Tie Guan Yin is treasured as an authentic living preservation of classic oolong craftsmanship that has become scarce in its ancestral homeland.
interestingFacts: Muzha is located right within the metropolitan boundaries of Taipei, making it one of the very few commercial tea terroirs nestled inside a world capital.
Comparing modern mainland Anxi Tie Guan Yin with Muzha Tie Guan Yin provides a textbook demonstration of how processing methods diverge over history from identical cultivars.
